The purpose of the contribution is to establish MidPC as the best-performing SVD-based initialization for reducing forgetting in continual learning. Paper [9] discusses specialized LoRA initialization to alleviate catastrophic forgetting, which is conceptually similar but does not specifically establish MidPC as the best-performing SVD-based initialization. Paper [16] introduces PiSSA, which also uses SVD-based initialization for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, but it does not focus on reducing forgetting as the primary goal. Paper [23] introduces SILoR, another SVD-based initialization for low-rank adaptation, but its focus is on computational efficiency rather than reducing forgetting. None of the prior papers explicitly establish MidPC as the best-performing SVD-based initialization for reducing forgetting.

The mechanism involves benchmarking MidPC against PiSSA and MiLoRA on forgetting and backward-transfer metrics. Paper [16] introduces PiSSA, which is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method using SVD-based initialization, and Paper [9] discusses LoRA initialization methods to mitigate forgetting. Paper [23] introduces SILoR, another SVD-based initialization for low-rank adaptation. These papers describe mechanisms that are substantively equivalent to the mechanism in the contribution, as they all involve SVD-based initialization methods for parameter-efficient fine-tuning and address forgetting or related metrics.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves comparing forgetting and backward-transfer metrics across MidPC, PiSSA, and MiLoRA. Paper [6] evaluates continual learning methods using backward knowledge transfer metrics, which is substantively equivalent to the evaluation design in the contribution. Paper [16] evaluates PiSSA using forgetting metrics, which also matches the evaluation design. Paper [25] conducts an empirical study on forgetting in low-rank decomposition-based fine-tuning, which includes similar metrics and evaluation designs. Thus, the evaluation design is covered by prior work.

The domain of the contribution is continual learning of large language models (LLMs). Papers [6], [9], [16], and [25] all address continual learning in the context of large language models or parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods for LLMs. Therefore, the domain is covered.
